## Teaching philosophy {#philosophy}

My primary goal as an instructor is to make sure every student feels safe, welcome,
and respected, and knows they belong in the mathematics classroom. Students arrive
with very different experiences of mathematics, and some have had far more support
and encouragement than others. I share the conviction behind Federico
Ardila-Mantilla's axioms for mathematics education: mathematical talent is
distributed equally across groups of people, and every student deserves meaningful
mathematical experiences and to be treated with dignity and respect.

My own interest in mathematics took time to develop. As a child I struggled with
mathematics and physics, but I still vividly remember the experiments shown to us by
a physics teacher who made a two-hour journey through Indian city traffic to teach our
weekend classes. That teacher showed me how much an instructor can do by making room
for curiosity and believing that students can understand. His example is why I
volunteer with math circles and with science and mathematics camps for girls.

::: {.pullquote}
Students should *do* mathematics, not just watch it; they should do it *together*;
and they should be cared for as *whole people*.

[The three commitments that run through my teaching]{.pullquote-cite}
:::

## Principles in practice {#principles}

::: {.principle-grid}
::: {.principle-card}
[1]{.principle-num}

### Doing mathematics, not just watching it

After introducing a concept and working an example, I give students time to try a
related problem before I present a solution. I circulate, offering small hints and
asking questions that help them find a next step. When a student is unsure or makes a
mistake, my first concern is to help them feel at ease: an incomplete idea is still
worth discussing, and I openly acknowledge my own mistakes.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
[2]{.principle-num}

### Finding the right picture

A good picture often makes sense before a formal statement does. In MTH 314, I used
geometric transformations of the plane so that students understood what eigenvalues
and eigenvectors tell us about a linear transformation while they learned to compute
them.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
[3]{.principle-num}

### Learning together

Explaining an idea to a classmate is one of the best ways to understand it, and asking
a classmate is often easier than asking the instructor. I build group work into class
time in person, and I design online courses so that live sessions are spent working
together.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
[4]{.principle-num}

### Caring for the whole student

My students have lives and pressures outside my course. I offer flexible deadlines in
difficult circumstances, space exams so students have time to prepare, and avoid
scheduling an exam right after a long weekend or break. An exam is a fair measure of
learning only when students have had a fair chance to prepare.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
[5]{.principle-num}

### Mistakes as a reason to keep working

Standards-based grading in MTH 103A gave students further opportunities to show
mastery of topics they first found difficult, so an unsuccessful attempt became a
reason to keep working rather than a final verdict.
:::

::: {.principle-card}
[6]{.principle-num}

### Not waiting for students to come to me

In an online course a struggling student can easily go unnoticed. In MTH 314 I wrote
to students who were not doing well and met with them individually on Zoom.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Using AI to sharpen proof reading.** In MTH 317H recitations I give students poorly
written AI-generated proofs and ask them to find unjustified assumptions, missing
steps, and errors that are easy to overlook when an explanation sounds convincing, and
to say what the AI did well. The aim is for students to understand its possibilities
and limits, and to gain the confidence to assess an argument for themselves, not to
have AI do their homework.
:::

## Teaching across course contexts {#contexts}

::: {.context-grid}
::: {.context-card}
### MTH 103A: College Algebra I
*Instructor of record · Spring 2025 · about 60 students*

Taught in an active-learning classroom in the MSU Union, with round tables and screens
throughout the room. Students worked in groups while two undergraduate learning
assistants and I circulated, and I wrote live on an iPad projected to every table. The
class met daily at 8 a.m. through a Michigan winter, so I offered a Zoom option for
icy mornings and possible closures. I wrote my own lecture notes and worksheets and
used standards-based grading.
:::

::: {.context-card}
### MTH 124: Survey of Calculus
*Instructor of record · Summer 2023 · fully online*

Structured as a flipped classroom. Students watched videos I recorded before class,
meeting new ideas at their own pace, so live sessions could be spent working problems
together and consolidating the theory. The course ran on Piazza with engagement
points, and students could optionally make a short "reel" introducing themselves to
help them find classmates to work with.
:::

::: {.context-card}
### MTH 314: Matrix Algebra with Applications
*Instructor of record · Summer 2024 · fully online*

I wrote lecture notes in LaTeX and also shared the handwritten notes produced live in
each Zoom lecture, so students had both a polished reference and a record of how each
argument unfolded. I recorded lecture videos, posted short check-in videos between
meetings, and designed in-class Python assignments so students practiced the
computational side of matrix algebra alongside the theory.
:::

::: {.context-card}
### MTH 317H: Honors Linear Algebra
*Recitation leader · Fall 2026*

I teach the proof techniques from MTH 299 that students need but may not yet know,
with worksheets that ask *why* a concept is useful or needed. Complete solutions are
released twenty-four hours after each deadline so students can check their reasoning.
[Course materials →](mth317h-fs26.qmd)
:::
:::

I have also been instructor of record for MTH 234: Multivariable Calculus (Fall 2024),
and a teaching assistant for courses including MTH 299 (Introduction to Proofs) and
MTH 818 (Graduate Algebra I). See the full list on the [Teaching](../teaching.qmd) page.

## Leadership and mentoring {#leadership}

- **Lead Teaching Assistant**, MSU (Fall 2024, Spring 2025): observed classrooms and
  gave teaching feedback to 8 teaching assistants and 16 undergraduate learning
  assistants.
- **Mentor**, MSU Summer Topology Program (Summer 2026): supervised two undergraduate
  projects, on Euler characteristics and the Lefschetz fixed-point theorem, and on the
  Gauss–Bonnet theorem and the classification of surfaces.
- **Tutor and Supervisor**, Mathematics Learning Center (6+ semesters).
- **Panelist**, orientation for incoming Ph.D. students (Fall 2024).
- **Outreach**: volunteer with math circles and with science and mathematics camps for
  girls.

## Professional development {#cct}

I am completing MSU's
[Certification in College Teaching](https://grad.msu.edu/professional-development/graduate-educator-advancement-and-teaching/certification-in-college-teaching)
(expected Spring 2027), including the course **MTHE 879: Teaching College
Mathematics**.

**Certification in College Teaching Institute workshops attended (May 2026)**

- *Understanding the University Context: Aligning Teaching with Different Institutional
  Types and Missions*, Dr. Judith Stoddart (Vice Provost, University Arts and Collections)
- *Creating Effective Learning Environments*, Dr. Kirstin Parkin (Associate Professor,
  Microbiology and Molecular Genetics)
- *Assessing Student Learning*, Dr. Rique Campa (Professor and Senior Associate Dean,
  Graduate School)
- *Incorporating Technology in Teaching*, Dr. Stefanie Baier

**Looking ahead.** Conversations with classmates from several disciplines have
encouraged me to give students more choice in how they show understanding. Where a
course allows it, I would like to offer projects such as a video, artwork, or a
physical model, like a toy that demonstrates projectile motion for a unit on
quadratics.

**Free tools and texts**

- [Desmos](https://www.desmos.com/calculator): online graphing calculator

- [*Book of Proof*](https://richardhammack.github.io/BookOfProof/) by Richard Hammack
- [*Linear Algebra Done Right*](https://linear.axler.net) by Sheldon Axler, and
  [*Linear Algebra Done Wrong*](https://www.math.brown.edu/streil/papers/LADW/LADW.html)
  by Sergei Treil
- [Overleaf](https://www.overleaf.com): write mathematics in LaTeX in the browser
